items.title: Biggest crash cause: missed risk
items.simple: The biggest cause of crashes is missing a risk. Keep looking ahead, to the sides and behind you. Know where other cars are. Watch for people walking and riding bikes.
items.official: The single biggest contributor to crashes is failing to identify a risk. Always know where other vehicles are positioned around you. You must look down the road, to the sides, and behind your vehicle. You must also be alert for unexpected events, especially pedestrians and bicyclists.

items.title: Headlights at 500-foot visibility
items.simple: Rain, fog, snow or sleet can make it hard to see. If you can see only 500 feet ahead, you must turn on your headlights. It is the law.
items.official: Virginia law requires motorists to use headlights during inclement weather such as rain, fog, snow or sleet when visibility is reduced to 500 feet.

items.title: Wipers on means headlights on
items.simple: If your wipers are on because of bad weather, your headlights must be on too. Headlights help other drivers see you, even in the daytime.
items.official: You must use your headlights whenever you use your windshield wipers as a result of bad weather. Using headlights at all times, including during the day, increases your vehicle's visibility.

items.title: Headlights whenever it's hard to see
items.simple: You must use your headlights at night. You must also use them at other times when it is hard to see.
items.official: You must use your headlights at night and at other times when it's hard to see.

items.title: Bad conditions: slow down first
items.simple: It is risky to drive when you can't see well. It is risky when rain, snow or ice covers the road. Your first move is to slow down. Then turn on your headlights.
items.official: Driving becomes hazardous when visibility is reduced or when the road surface is covered with rain, snow or ice. Reducing your speed should be your first response to decreased visibility and dangerous road conditions. Turn on your headlights.

items.title: Double your following distance
items.simple: In bad weather or on a slick road, leave twice your normal space behind the car ahead. More space gives you more time to stop.
items.official: Increase your space cushion by doubling your normal following distance.

items.title: Headlights from sunset to sunrise
items.simple: Turn on your headlights at sunset, as soon as it starts to get dark. Keep them on until sunrise. This helps other drivers see you.
items.official: At sunset, as soon as light begins to fade, turn on your headlights to make your vehicle more visible to others. You must use headlights from sunset to sunrise.
items.mnemonic: Sun goes down, lights go on.

items.title: Low beams in town, for oncoming
items.simple: Use low beams in cities and towns, unless the street has no lights. When a car is coming toward you, switch to low beams so you don't blind the driver.
items.official: Use low-beams when driving in cities and towns, except on streets where there is no lighting. Switch to low-beams whenever you meet oncoming traffic to avoid blinding the other driver.

items.title: Following: low beams within 200 feet
items.simple: When you are driving behind a car at night, use your low beams once you are within 200 feet of it.
items.official: When following, use low-beams whenever you are within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead.
items.mnemonic: Behind a car: 200 feet. Car coming at you: 500 feet.

items.title: High beams: dim within 500 feet
items.simple: On dark highways, you can use high beams. When a car is coming toward you and gets within 500 feet, switch to low beams.
items.official: Use high-beam headlights on highways, unless another vehicle is within 500 feet coming toward you.
items.mnemonic: Behind a car: 200 feet. Car coming at you: 500 feet.

items.title: Bright oncoming lights: look aside
items.simple: If a car coming at you has bright high beams, do not stare at the lights. Glance at the side of the road, then look ahead. Repeat this until you pass the car. Keep your own high beams off.
items.official: If the high-beams of an oncoming car are on, avoid looking directly at the bright lights. Glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead to determine the other vehicle's position. Keep doing this until you have passed the other vehicle. Even if the other driver does not dim his headlights, do not turn on your high-beam headlights.

items.title: Fog: low beams, edge, slow
items.simple: Fog bounces light back into your eyes. Use low beams, not high beams. Follow the lines at the edge of the road. Even light fog makes distance hard to judge, so slow down.
items.official: Fog reflects light and can reflect your own headlights back into your eyes. Use low-beam headlights in heavy fog and look for road edge markings to guide you. Even light fog reduces visibility and your ability to judge distances, so slow down.
items.mnemonic: Fog: go low, find the edge, go slow.

items.title: Rain: low beams, check blind spots
items.simple: Heavy rain can be as risky as fog, especially when it is windy. Cars behind you and in your blind spots are hard to see. Use low beams to see and be seen.
items.official: Driving in heavy rain can be as hazardous as driving in fog, especially if the wind is blowing. Other vehicles to the rear and in blind spot areas are especially difficult to see when it's raining. Use your low-beam headlights to see and be seen.

items.title: Wipers and washer fluid
items.simple: In light rain or drizzle, turn on your wipers to see better. Using wipers for just a few sprinkles can smear the windshield. Keep washer fluid in your car.
items.official: In light rain or drizzle, turn on your windshield wipers to improve visibility; using wipers for sprinkles may smear the windshield and make it harder to see, so make sure you have windshield washer fluid.

items.title: First half hour of rain
items.simple: When rain has just started, the road is extra slippery for the first half hour. Oil on the road mixes with the water. Slow down and take care.
items.official: When rain begins, during the first half-hour, roads are more likely to be slippery due to oil on the road surface mixing with water.
items.mnemonic: First 30 minutes of rain: oil slick.

items.title: Avoid ponded water
items.simple: Standing water on the road can make your car hydroplane (slide on the water). You can lose control. Go around it if you can. If you cannot, drive with care.
items.official: Use caution when driving through ponded water, and avoid it if possible. Ponded water can cause vehicles to hydroplane or otherwise lose control.

items.title: Clear all snow before driving
items.simple: Before you drive, clear all snow and ice off your car. That includes the roof, hood, back, windows, mirrors and lights. Snow that flies off is a danger to other drivers. Snow tires or chains help stop skids.
items.official: Remove snow and ice from your entire car, including the roof, hood and rear of the vehicle, before you start driving. Snow and ice left on the car can fly off and create a hazard for other motorists. Clear all of your windows, mirrors and front and rear lights. Equip your car with all-weather snow tires or chains to help prevent skidding and reduce stopping distance.

items.title: Ice or packed snow: brake gently
items.simple: Packed snow is like ice. To stop, take your foot off the gas. Then brake gently. Slow down before you stop or turn. Your front tires grip best while they keep rolling.
items.official: Driving on packed snow is similar to driving on ice. When you brake, apply the brakes gently. Slow down before stopping or turning. When driving on slippery surfaces and you need to stop, release the accelerator and apply brakes gently. You have the most traction and control when the front tires are rolling. Keeping a slow, steady speed, rather than hard braking, will allow you to control your vehicle.
items.mnemonic: On ice: gentle feet, rolling wheels.

items.title: Bridges freeze first
items.simple: Bridges freeze before other parts of the road. Shady spots can have ice too. In cold weather, slow down before a bridge.
items.official: Watch for ice on bridges and in shady areas. Bridges freeze before other road surfaces.

items.title: Deer: dusk and dawn, fall
items.simple: Watch for deer at dusk and dawn, most of all in the fall. A Deer Crossing sign means deer cross the road here. Slow down and be ready to stop.
items.official: Be alert at dusk and dawn especially in the fall. Deer Crossing: Deer cross the roadway in this area. Slow down, be alert and be ready to stop.
items.mnemonic: Deer at dusk, dawn and fall.

items.title: Deer near road: slow, honk
items.simple: If you see a deer near the road, slow down. Deer often travel in groups, so more are likely nearby. Use your horn to scare it away.
items.official: Slow down if you see a large animal near or crossing the road. Large animals frequently travel in groups; there are likely others nearby. Use the horn to scare the animal away.

items.title: Can't miss the deer? Don't swerve
items.simple: If you cannot avoid hitting a deer, do not swerve. Brake firmly, stay in your lane and come to a controlled stop. If you hit it, tell the police.
items.official: If a collision with a deer or other animal is unavoidable, do not swerve. Brake firmly, stay in your lane, and come to a controlled stop. If you hit a large animal, report it to law enforcement.

items.title: Crash: stop, clear the road
items.simple: After a crash, you must stop at the scene or close to it. Do not block traffic. If no one is hurt and the cars can move, move them off the road. Get out of your car carefully.
items.official: Stop at the scene of the crash or as close to the scene as possible without blocking traffic. Drivers must move vehicles from the road immediately if the vehicles are able to be moved, no one is injured and the driver is capable of safely doing so. Be careful when exiting your vehicle. Keep your vehicle between you and moving traffic if possible.

items.title: Help the injured, don't move them
items.simple: Give any help you can to anyone who is hurt. Do not pull them out of the car. Move them only if there is danger, such as fire, or if you have medical training.
items.official: Give any help you can if someone is injured. Do not attempt to move an injured person from a wrecked vehicle unless you have the necessary medical training or there is an immediate danger such as fire.

items.title: Report crashes to police
items.simple: Tell the police about a crash as soon as you can. You must report any crash with damage, injury or death.
items.official: Report the crash to the police as quickly as possible. Motor vehicle crashes involving property damage, personal injury or death must be reported to the police.

items.title: Swap info, call your insurance
items.simple: After a crash, exchange information. Get each driver's name, address, license number and plate number. Get the names and addresses of anyone hurt and of witnesses. Get each owner's insurance policy number. Then call your insurance company.
items.official: Exchange information with other people involved in the crash as soon as possible: name, address and driver's license number of other drivers; license plate numbers of other vehicles; name and address of anyone who was injured; name and address of each witness; name, address and insurance policy number of other vehicle owners. Notify your insurance company immediately.

items.title: DMV crash report: over $3,000
items.simple: Police must send a written crash report to DMV if anyone is hurt or killed. They also send one if the damage is more than $3,000. The crash goes on each driver's record.
items.official: Law enforcement officers are required to forward a written crash report to DMV when a traffic crash results in injury or the death of any person or total property damage is in excess of $3,000. All crash information will be recorded on the DMV records of each driver involved in the crash.
items.mnemonic: Hurt, killed, or over $3,000: DMV gets a report.

items.title: Parked car hit: note, report
items.simple: If you hit a parked car with no one in it, try to find the owner. If you cannot, leave a note. Write your name, phone number, the date, the time and the damage. Tell the police within 24 hours.
items.official: You must make a reasonable effort to find the owner of an unattended vehicle or other property damaged in a crash. If you cannot locate anyone, leave a note that can be found easily at the scene of the crash. Include your name, telephone number, the date and time of the crash, and a description of the damage. You must also report the crash to the police within 24 hours.
items.mnemonic: No owner? Leave a note. Tell police within 24 hours.

items.title: Police stop: pull over, stay in
items.simple: If a police officer stops you, stay calm. Pull to the side of the road in a safe place and park. Stay in your car unless the officer asks you to get out.
items.official: If you are stopped by a police officer: Remain calm. Pull your vehicle to the side of the road in a safe location and park. Stay in your vehicle. Do not get out unless the officer asks you to.

items.title: Police stop: flashers, inside light
items.simple: After you pull over for police, turn on your flashers. At night, also turn on the light inside your car.
items.official: Turn on your flashers. If you are pulled over at night, turn on your vehicle's interior lights.

items.title: Police stop: engine off, window down
items.simple: Turn off your engine and radio. Turn off anything that makes it hard to talk. Roll down your window. The officer may walk up on either side of your car.
items.official: Turn off your engine, radio, and any other device that could block communication with the officer. Roll down your window so that you can communicate with the officer. An officer may approach your vehicle on the driver or passenger side for safety reasons.

items.title: Police stop: belts on, hands seen
items.simple: Keep your seat belt on. Keep your hands on the wheel, where the officer can see them. Do not reach around. If asked for your papers, say where they are. Reach for them slowly, with one hand on the wheel.
items.official: Keep your safety belt fastened and ask your passengers to keep their belts fastened. Keep your hands in plain view, preferably on the steering wheel. Ask your passengers to keep their hands in plain view also. Do not make any movement that will make the officer think you are hiding or reaching for something. If the officer asks for your license, registration and insurance documents, tell him where they are and reach for them slowly, keeping one hand on the steering wheel.

items.title: Carry license, registration, insurance
items.simple: Always carry three things when you drive. You need your driver's license and proof that your car is registered. You also need proof of insurance. An officer may ask to see them.
items.official: Carry proper identification: a valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration and proof of insurance.
items.mnemonic: 3 papers: you (license), your car (registration), your coverage (insurance).

items.title: Unmarked car: ask for ID
items.simple: If the officer is in an unmarked car or is not in uniform, you may ask to see the officer's ID.
items.official: If the officer is driving an unmarked car or is not in uniform, you may ask to see his or her identification.

items.title: Sign the ticket; argue in court
items.simple: Answer the officer's questions clearly. If you disagree, do not argue now. You can make your case in court. Sign the ticket. Signing does not mean you admit guilt.
items.official: Answer the officer's questions fully and clearly. If you disagree with the officer, do not discuss your point of view at that time. You will have your chance to make your case in court. Sign the citation; this is not an admission of guilt. Refusal to sign the citation may result in your arrest. Or, you may be required to go to the police station.

events.prompt: If you disagree with the officer, what should you do?
events.missLine: Stay calm during the stop. You can make your case in court.

questions.prompt: What is the single biggest cause of crashes?
questions.explain: The single biggest cause of crashes is failing to identify a risk.

questions.prompt: Where should you look to know where other vehicles are around you?
choices: Only at the car in front of you
Down the road, to the sides and behind your vehicle
At the road just in front of your hood
questions.explain: You must look down the road, to the sides and behind your vehicle.

questions.prompt: In bad weather, Virginia law requires headlights when visibility is reduced to what distance?
questions.explain: Virginia law requires headlights in rain, fog, snow or sleet when visibility is reduced to 500 feet.

questions.prompt: Which of these can reduce visibility to 500 feet and require you to turn on your headlights?
questions.explain: Virginia law requires headlights in bad weather such as rain, fog, snow or sleet when visibility is reduced to 500 feet.

questions.prompt: What must you also do when you use your windshield wipers because of bad weather?
questions.explain: You must use your headlights whenever you use your wipers because of bad weather.

questions.prompt: What is true about using your headlights at all times, even during the day?
questions.explain: Using headlights at all times, including during the day, increases your vehicle's visibility.

questions.prompt: When must you use your headlights?
choices: At night and at other times when it is hard to see
Only when other cars have their headlights on
questions.explain: You must use your headlights at night and at other times when it is hard to see.

questions.prompt: It is daytime, but it has become hard to see the road. What should you do?
choices: Wait until sunset to turn on your headlights
Turn on your high beams in traffic
questions.explain: You must use your headlights at night and at other times when it is hard to see.

questions.prompt: What should be your first response to reduced visibility or dangerous road conditions?
questions.explain: Your first response to reduced visibility and dangerous road conditions should be to reduce your speed.

questions.prompt: Which of these can make driving hazardous?
choices: A road covered with rain, snow or ice
questions.explain: Driving becomes hazardous when visibility is reduced or when the road is covered with rain, snow or ice.

questions.prompt: What should you do to increase your space cushion when visibility is reduced or the road is slippery?
choices: Follow closer so you can see taillights
questions.explain: In hazardous conditions, double your normal following distance. More space gives you more time to stop.

questions.prompt: What should your following distance be on a snowy or icy road?
choices: The same as on a dry road
As close as needed to see the car ahead
questions.explain: When the road is covered with snow or ice, double your normal following distance.

questions.prompt: When must you use your headlights?
questions.explain: You must use your headlights from sunset to sunrise.

questions.prompt: What should you do at sunset, when the light begins to fade?
choices: Wait until it is fully dark
Turn on your high beams in town
questions.explain: As soon as the light begins to fade, turn on your headlights so others can see you.

questions.prompt: Which lights should you use when you drive at night on lighted streets in cities and towns?
questions.explain: Use low beams in cities and towns, except on streets that have no lighting.

questions.prompt: In which of these situations should you always switch to low-beam headlights?
choices: When you drive on an empty, unlit highway
When you pass a parked car
When you enter a well-lit parking lot
questions.explain: Switch to low beams whenever you meet oncoming traffic so you do not blind the other driver.

questions.prompt: Why should you dim your headlights for oncoming traffic?
choices: To avoid blinding the other driver
To signal that you will turn
questions.explain: Switch to low beams for oncoming traffic so that you do not blind the other driver.

questions.prompt: You are following another vehicle at night. Within what distance of it should you use low beams?
questions.explain: When you follow a vehicle, use low beams whenever you are within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead.

questions.prompt: You are driving at night and come within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead. What should you do?
questions.explain: Use low beams when you are within 200 feet of the vehicle you are following.

questions.prompt: On a highway at night, you must dim your high beams when an oncoming vehicle is within what distance?
questions.explain: Use high beams on highways unless an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet.

questions.prompt: When should you use high-beam headlights?
choices: In cities and towns, on lighted streets
On highways, unless an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet
When you are within 200 feet of the vehicle ahead
questions.explain: Use high beams on highways, unless another vehicle is within 500 feet coming toward you.

questions.prompt: You are using high beams on a dark highway. A car coming toward you is less than 500 feet away. What should you do?
questions.explain: Dim your high beams to low beams when an oncoming vehicle is within 500 feet.

questions.prompt: If an oncoming driver has high beams on, what should you do?
choices: Look directly at the oncoming lights
Turn on your own high beams
Glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead
Stop in your lane until the car passes
questions.explain: Avoid looking at the bright lights. Glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead.

questions.prompt: An oncoming driver does not dim his high beams. What should you do?
choices: Turn on your high beams to warn him
Flash your high beams until he dims his lights
questions.explain: Do not turn on your high beams, even if the other driver does not dim his headlights.

questions.prompt: The glare from an oncoming car's high beams bothers you. You glance toward the side of the road, then ahead. How long should you keep doing this?
choices: Until you have passed the other vehicle
Until you can flash your lights
questions.explain: Glance toward the side of the road, then look quickly ahead. Keep doing this until you have passed the other vehicle.

questions.prompt: What should you use when you drive in heavy fog?
questions.explain: Use low-beam headlights in heavy fog, because fog can reflect your own headlights back into your eyes.

questions.prompt: In heavy fog, what should you look for to guide you?
choices: The taillights of the car ahead
questions.explain: In heavy fog, look for road edge markings to guide you.

questions.prompt: Why should you slow down even in light fog?
choices: Fog reduces visibility and your ability to judge distances
Fog makes your engine run hot
questions.explain: Even light fog reduces visibility and your ability to judge distances, so you should slow down.

questions.prompt: Why are high-beam headlights a poor choice in fog?
choices: Fog reflects your own light back into your eyes
They make your car harder to see
questions.explain: Fog reflects light and can reflect your own headlights back into your eyes.

questions.prompt: What should you use when you drive in rain?
questions.explain: Use your low-beam headlights in rain so that you can see and be seen.

questions.prompt: When it is raining, which vehicles are especially hard to see?
choices: Vehicles directly in front of you
Vehicles behind you and in your blind spots
Vehicles stopped at a red light
questions.explain: Vehicles behind you and in your blind spots are especially hard to see in the rain.

questions.prompt: Driving in heavy rain can be as hazardous as driving in fog. When is it especially hazardous?
choices: When you are using low beams
When you are on a city street
questions.explain: Heavy rain can be as hazardous as fog, especially if the wind is blowing.

questions.prompt: Using wipers for only a few sprinkles may smear the windshield. What should you do about this?
choices: Never use wipers in light rain
Make sure you have windshield washer fluid
questions.explain: Wipers used for sprinkles may smear the windshield, so make sure you have washer fluid.

questions.prompt: What should you do in light rain or drizzle?
choices: Wait for heavy rain before using wipers
Turn on your windshield wipers to see better
questions.explain: In light rain or drizzle, turn on your windshield wipers to see better.

questions.prompt: When rain begins, for how long are the roads more likely to be slippery?
questions.explain: Roads are more likely to be slippery during the first half hour of rain.

questions.prompt: Why are roads more slippery right after rain begins?
choices: Oil on the road surface mixes with water
questions.explain: Oil on the road surface mixes with water when rain begins, which makes the road slippery.

questions.prompt: You see this sign, and rain has just begun. What should you do?
choices: Speed up to get out of the rain
Slow down, because the road may be extra slippery
Brake hard to test the road
questions.explain: This sign warns that the road is slippery. Roads are more likely to be slippery in the first half hour of rain.

questions.prompt: What can ponded water on the road cause your vehicle to do?
questions.explain: Ponded water can cause vehicles to hydroplane or otherwise lose control.

questions.prompt: What should you do when you see ponded water on the road?
choices: Speed up to get through it quickly
Brake hard in the middle of it
Avoid it if possible, or use caution
questions.explain: Use caution when you drive through ponded water, and avoid it if possible.

questions.prompt: After a snowfall, which parts of your car should you clear of snow and ice before you drive?
choices: Your entire car, including the roof, hood, back, windows, mirrors and lights
Only the front and rear lights
questions.explain: Remove snow and ice from your entire car before you start driving.

questions.prompt: How do all-weather snow tires or chains help?
choices: They prevent skidding and reduce stopping distance
They make it safe to follow closely
They remove the need to slow down
questions.explain: Snow tires or chains help prevent skidding and reduce stopping distance.

questions.prompt: Why should you clear snow off your roof before driving?
choices: It can fly off and create a hazard for other drivers
It is needed to open your doors
questions.explain: Snow and ice left on the car can fly off and create a hazard for other drivers.

questions.prompt: You are driving on an icy or slippery road and have to stop. What should you do?
choices: Apply the brakes in a normal way
Release the gas and apply the brakes gently
questions.explain: On slippery surfaces, release the accelerator and apply the brakes gently.

questions.prompt: On slippery surfaces, when do you have the most traction and control?
choices: When your front tires are rolling
When your front tires are locked
When your front tires are turned sharply
When your front tires are spinning fast
questions.explain: You have the most traction and control when the front tires are rolling.

questions.prompt: Driving on packed snow is similar to driving on which surface?
questions.explain: Driving on packed snow is similar to driving on ice.

questions.prompt: On a slippery road, what helps you control your vehicle best?
questions.explain: A slow, steady speed, rather than hard braking, lets you control your vehicle.

questions.prompt: Which road surface freezes before other road surfaces?
questions.explain: Bridges freeze before other road surfaces.

questions.prompt: In freezing weather, when or where should you watch especially for ice?
choices: On bridges and in shady areas
questions.explain: Watch for ice on bridges and in shady areas. Bridges freeze before other road surfaces.

questions.prompt: You see this sign at dusk in the fall. What should you do?
choices: Speed up to get past the area
Slow down, be alert and be ready to stop
Use the shoulder to drive around animals
questions.explain: Deer cross the road in this area, so slow down, be alert and be ready to stop. Watch for deer especially at dusk and dawn in the fall.

questions.prompt: When or where should you be especially alert for deer and other large animals?
choices: At dusk and dawn, especially in the fall
questions.explain: Be alert at dusk and dawn, especially in the fall.

questions.prompt: You see a deer cross the road ahead. What should you do?
choices: Speed up before more deer come
Slow down, because other deer are likely nearby
Stop and get out of your car
questions.explain: Slow down, because large animals often travel in groups and others are likely nearby.

questions.prompt: What can you do to scare a deer or other large animal away from the road?
questions.explain: Use your horn to scare the animal away.

questions.prompt: You pass this sign, and one deer runs across the road. What should you expect?
choices: The deer will stay off the road
questions.explain: Large animals often travel in groups, so other deer are likely nearby.

questions.prompt: If you cannot avoid hitting a deer, what should you do?
choices: Swerve into the next lane to miss it
Speed up to get past it
Brake firmly, stay in your lane, and come to a controlled stop
questions.explain: Do not swerve. Brake firmly, stay in your lane, and come to a controlled stop.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you hit a large animal?
choices: Report it only if your car is damaged
questions.explain: If you hit a large animal, report it to law enforcement.

questions.prompt: What must you do if you are involved in a crash?
choices: Take the injured person to the nearest hospital
Continue home and file a crash report
Stop, help the injured, report the crash to the police, exchange information, and tell your insurance company
Check your car for damage and leave
questions.explain: After a crash, you must stop, help the injured, report to the police, exchange information, and notify your insurance company.

questions.prompt: After a crash, no one is hurt and the vehicles can be moved. What must the drivers do?
choices: Move the vehicles off the road right away if it is safe to do so
Leave the vehicles where they are until the police arrive
questions.explain: Drivers must move their vehicles off the road right away if the vehicles can be moved, no one is hurt, and it is safe.

questions.prompt: What should you do when you get out of your car after a crash?
choices: Stand in the lane to warn others
Stand behind your car in the lane
Keep your vehicle between you and moving traffic if you can
questions.explain: Be careful when you get out. Keep your vehicle between you and moving traffic if you can.

questions.prompt: When may you move an injured person out of a wrecked vehicle?
choices: When you want to drive the person home
When there is immediate danger, such as fire, or you have medical training
When the person asks for water
questions.explain: Do not move an injured person unless there is immediate danger, such as fire, or you have medical training.

questions.prompt: What should you do at a crash scene where someone is injured?
choices: Pull the person out of the car right away
Move the person into your car
Give any help you can, without moving the person unless there is immediate danger
questions.explain: Give any help you can, but do not move an injured person unless there is immediate danger or you have medical training.

questions.prompt: What is the rule for crashes that involve property damage, personal injury, or death?
choices: They do not need to be reported
They need to be reported only to your insurance company
They must be reported to the police
They must be reported only if someone is killed
questions.explain: A crash that involves property damage, personal injury, or death must be reported to the police.

questions.prompt: When must you report a traffic crash to the police?
choices: You must report it as quickly as possible
You must report it within 30 days
You must report it only if the other driver asks
You must report it only if your car cannot be driven
questions.explain: You must report the crash to the police as quickly as possible.

questions.prompt: What should you get from the other drivers after a crash?
choices: Their name, address, and driver's license number
questions.explain: You should get the name, address, and driver's license number of each other driver.

questions.prompt: What should you get from the owners of the other vehicles in a crash?
choices: Their name, address, and insurance policy number
questions.explain: You should get the name, address, and insurance policy number of the other vehicle owners.

questions.prompt: When should you notify your insurance company after a crash?
choices: You should notify it within one year
You should notify it only if you were at fault
You should notify it only if the police tell you to
questions.explain: You should notify your insurance company immediately after a crash.

questions.prompt: Officers must send a written crash report to DMV when total property damage is more than what amount?
questions.explain: Officers send a written crash report to DMV when property damage is more than $3,000, or when someone is injured or killed.

questions.prompt: Where is crash information recorded?
choices: Only on the record of the driver who was at fault
On the DMV records of each driver involved
On a DMV record only if someone is hurt
Only on the vehicle owner's record
questions.explain: All crash information is recorded on the DMV records of each driver involved in the crash.

questions.prompt: When must a law enforcement officer forward a written crash report to DMV?
choices: When a crash causes any damage at all
When a crash causes damage only to a mailbox
When a crash causes a flat tire
When a crash causes any injury or death
questions.explain: Officers forward a crash report to DMV when anyone is injured or killed, or when property damage is more than $3,000.

questions.prompt: You damage an unattended vehicle and cannot find the owner. You must leave a note. How soon must you also report the crash to the police?
questions.explain: You must report the crash to the police within 24 hours.

questions.prompt: What must a note include if you leave one on an unattended vehicle that you damaged?
choices: Your name, telephone number, the date and time of the crash, and a description of the damage
questions.explain: The note must include your name, telephone number, the date and time of the crash, and a description of the damage.

questions.prompt: You hit a parked car, and no one is around. What must you do first?
choices: Drive away if the damage is small
Make a reasonable effort to find the owner
questions.explain: You must make a reasonable effort to find the owner of an unattended vehicle that you damage.

questions.prompt: What should you do if a police officer stops you?
choices: Get out and walk to the police car
Stay in your vehicle unless the officer asks you to get out
questions.explain: Stay in your vehicle. Do not get out unless the officer asks you to.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a police officer signals you to stop?
choices: Stay calm and pull to the side of the road in a safe place
Speed up to find a parking lot
questions.explain: Stay calm, pull to the side of the road in a safe place, and park.

questions.prompt: What should you do if police pull you over at night?
choices: Turn on the lights inside your car
questions.explain: If police pull you over at night, turn on the lights inside your car.

questions.prompt: What should you turn on after you pull over for a police officer?
questions.explain: Turn on your flashers when a police officer stops you.

questions.prompt: What should you do during a traffic stop?
choices: Keep your engine and radio on
Turn off your engine, radio, and other devices
questions.explain: Turn off your engine, your radio, and any device that could get in the way of talking with the officer.

questions.prompt: Why should you roll down your window during a traffic stop?
choices: So fresh air can come in
So the officer can reach your keys
So you can talk with the officer
questions.explain: You roll down your window so that you can talk with the officer.

questions.prompt: During a traffic stop, an officer may walk up to your vehicle:
choices: On the driver or passenger side
questions.explain: An officer may walk up to your vehicle on the driver side or the passenger side for safety reasons.

questions.prompt: What should you do with your hands during a traffic stop?
choices: Keep your hands in your pockets
Keep your hands under the seat
Keep your hands on the gear shift
Keep your hands in plain view, preferably on the steering wheel
questions.explain: Keep your hands in plain view, preferably on the steering wheel.

questions.prompt: What should you do when an officer asks for your license, registration, and proof of insurance?
choices: Tell the officer where the documents are, and reach for them slowly with one hand on the wheel
Quickly dig through your glove box
Get out and look in the trunk
questions.explain: Tell the officer where the documents are, and reach for them slowly with one hand on the steering wheel.

questions.prompt: What should you and your passengers do during a traffic stop?
choices: Unbuckle your safety belts to find your documents
questions.explain: You and your passengers should keep your safety belts fastened.

questions.prompt: What should your passengers do during a traffic stop?
choices: Keep their hands in plain view
Get out to talk to the officer
questions.explain: Ask your passengers to keep their hands in plain view and their belts fastened.

questions.prompt: What should you carry when you drive?
choices: Your license and your car title
A valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration, and proof of insurance
questions.explain: You should carry a valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration, and proof of insurance.

questions.prompt: A police officer stops you and asks for your documents. Which documents should you have with you?
choices: Your license, registration, and proof of insurance
questions.explain: You should carry a valid driver's license, proof of vehicle registration, and proof of insurance.

questions.prompt: If the officer who stops you is driving an unmarked car or is not in uniform, what may you do?
choices: Ask to see the officer's identification
questions.explain: If the officer is in an unmarked car or is not in uniform, you may ask to see the officer's identification.

questions.prompt: When may you ask to see a police officer's identification?
choices: When the officer is driving an unmarked car or is not in uniform
When the officer is in uniform and in a marked car
When the officer writes you a ticket
When the officer asks for your license
questions.explain: You may ask for identification if the officer is in an unmarked car or is not in uniform.

questions.prompt: What is true about signing a traffic citation?
choices: Signing it is an admission of guilt
Signing it is not an admission of guilt
Signing it is optional and has no effect
Signing it means you must pay right away
questions.explain: Sign the citation. Signing it is not an admission of guilt.

questions.prompt: What may happen if you refuse to sign a traffic citation?
questions.explain: If you refuse to sign the citation, you may be arrested.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you disagree with the officer during a traffic stop?
choices: Argue your point of view right away
Wait and make your case in court
Refuse to answer the officer's questions
questions.explain: Do not argue your point of view at the stop. You will have your chance to make your case in court.
